content: 1. The population subgroup analysis for race and ethnicity was not provided in the trials. Two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) reported no treatment interaction by race, but no data were included in the trials to support this. 2. Regarding regional economic development, no data were available. All trials were conducted in very high-income settings. 3. For older adults aged 60 years and over, no RCTs specifically restricted enrollment to this age group. Three RCTs reported no interaction by age. One trial indicated similar effects on pain intensity in individuals aged ≥65 years and those aged <65 years, with both groups showing an increased likelihood of experiencing ≥30% improvement in pain. However, two trials reported no interaction by age but did not provide supporting data. 4. The certainty of findings was downgraded for several reasons: Inconsistency: Downgraded one level when heterogeneity (I²) was high (e.g., I² = 68%, 78%, 67%, 73%, 58%, 72%). Risk of bias: Downgraded one level when trials were rated as fair or poor quality. Imprecision: Downgraded one or two levels when the number of participants was fewer than 100 or 200, or when confidence intervals crossed thresholds for small or large effects. Indirectness: Downgraded one level when heterogeneity (I²) was high (e.g., I² = 73%). 5. A single parallel randomized trial (Ionescu 2016) conducted in Romania evaluated the effects of tramadol (100 mg/day) for seven days compared to placebo in adults aged 20–60 years with chronic low back pain. Pain intensity was measured as a mean difference on a 1–6 visual analogue scale (transformed to 0–10) at seven days. The evidence was downgraded once for inconsistency (only one study, so consistency could not be assessed) and twice for imprecision (fewer than 100 participants). 6. For opioid analgesics used for less than one month to manage chronic primary low back pain, the evidence was limited to one trial. The certainty of findings was downgraded due to inconsistency and imprecision. 7. For nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) used for ≥12 weeks to manage chronic primary low back pain, the evidence was derived from three trials conducted in high-income countries. NSAIDs included naproxen (1100 mg/day), diflunisal (100 mg/day), flurbiprofen (300 mg/day), and indomethacin (150 mg/day). Pain intensity was measured at 2–3 weeks. The evidence was downgraded due to imputation of standard deviation in crossover trials and inconsistency (I² = 69%). 8. For NSAIDs used for <12 weeks, the evidence was based on two parallel trials conducted in high-income countries. NSAIDs included naproxen (1000 mg/day) and flupirtine modified release (400 mg/day). Pain intensity was measured at four weeks. The evidence was downgraded for inconsistency (only one study, so consistency could not be assessed) and imprecision (fewer than 200 participants). 9. The trials excluded patients with radicular leg pain, and no data were available for this subgroup. 10. The trials included adults with chronic low back pain, with mean ages ranging from 51 to 59 years. The evidence was downgraded for imprecision when pooled estimates crossed the null and thresholds for small or large effects. 11. References cited include studies by Berry et al. (1982), Ghosh et al. (1981), Gurrell et al. (2018), and Uberall et al. (2012), which evaluated various NSAIDs and their effects on chronic low back pain.
